records.title: George Washington (The "Port-hole" Portrait)
records.lender: Lent by The Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts, Philadelphia.
records.note: First president of the United States. When Peale painted this portrait in 1824, Washington had already become legendary. Peale created his likeness out of studies made when his father, Charles Willson Peale, had painted Washington nearly thirty years before. "I painted it," Peale said, "under the influence of extraordinary excitement and vivid recollection." And, as he had a good deal of P. T. Barnum in his nature, he immediately launched a campaign by lecture and pamphlet to have the new likeness accepted as the authentic national portrait in place of Stuart's "Athenaeum" head, which was then the favorite. As a made-up head, it cannot be accepted as a reliable portrait but its portrayal of Washington as a grandiose romantic hero shows how he appeared to the eyes of that time. It became very popular—by his own statement Peale painted seventy-nine replicas.

records.title: Andrew Jackson
records.lender: Lent by Mr. and Mrs. William A. Fisher, Detroit.
records.note: Seventh president of the United States. Painted in 1817 (three years after his defense of New Orleans made him the hero of the War of 1812) in the uniform of a Major-General. This is the best portrait of Old Hickory, showing the rugged character, the fiery temper and vitality of the Tennessee frontier aristocrat in most vivid fashion. Dated 1817.

records.title: John Quincy Adams
records.lender: Lent by the City of Boston, Massachusetts.
records.note: Sixth president of the United States, painted about 1844-47. This portrait is also that of a flinty character—a courageous, intelligent, acid, self-righteous man who spent his life in the nation's service. After the close of his one term as President he was elected to Congress in 1831 and served there until his death, becoming a great single-handed defender of the right of petition against the slavery party. "Mr. Adams chose wisely and according to his constitution," wrote Emerson in his Journal (1843), "when, on leaving the Presidency, he went into Congress. He is no literary old gentleman, but a bruiser, and loved the melée . . . He is an old roué who cannot live on slops, but must have sulphuric acid in his tea." Dated 1845.

records.title: John Charles Fremont
records.lender: Lent by The Brooklyn Museum, Brooklyn.
records.note: Explorer, soldier, politician, first candidate of the new Republican party in 1856 for the presidency, Fremont was a brilliant but unstable and undependable figure in our national life for several decades. His wife, Jessie Benton Fremont, is the subject of a current biography, Immortal Wife, by Irving Stone.

records.title: Captain Jean Terford David
records.lender: Lent by The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland.
records.section: The People — II. Elegance and Romantic Beauty
records.note: Sully was the great American master of decorative elegance in his portraits, of which these are outstanding examples. Jean Terford David was a French emigré who came to Philadelphia with his parents. He served in the American Army during the War of 1812; these portraits were painted in 1813. He married Mary Sicard of Philadelphia, whose father had also fled to America from France during the political troubles. Dated 1813.

records.title: Deliverance Mapes Waldo
records.lender: Lent by The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York City.
records.section: The People — II. Elegance and Romantic Beauty
records.note: The artist's second wife, painted about the time of her marriage in 1826. Dated about 1826.

records.title: Fanny Kemble as "Bianca"
records.lender: Lent by The Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, Philadelphia.
records.section: The People — II. Elegance and Romantic Beauty
records.note: Fanny Kemble belonged to a famous theatrical family which included her father Charles, her uncle John Kemble, and her aunt Mrs. Siddons. She came to the United States with her father in 1832. Her youth and beauty and the charm of her portrayal of Shakespeare's heroines were a national sensation. In spite of her talent she disliked the stage and although her marriage in 1834 with a Georgia planter, Pierce Butler, ended in divorce after a few years, she never returned to the stage. Dated about 1832-34.

records.title: Robert Fulton
records.lender: Lent by the Estate of Edsel B. Ford, Detroit.
records.note: Artist, engineer, inventor, one of the early outstanding examples of American mechanical ingenuity. His "Clermont" which steamed from New York to Albany on August 11, 1807, established the success of steamboat navigation in America. Dated about 1806-10.

records.title: Nathaniel Parker Willis
records.lender: Lent by The Morristown Library, Morristown, New Jersey.
records.note: Poet, essayist, editor, man of society. Willis was a writer of great fluency and popularity. He was popularly regarded in his own time as the leading American poet but his writings are now forgotten. He had great charm, which was both his strength and his weakness. This portrait was probably painted while Willis was in Boston in 1828 and 1829 as editor of the illustrated annals "The Legendary" and "The Token." Dated about 1828-29.

records.plate_caption: 10. NATHANIEL PARKER WILLIS by FRANCIS ALEXANDER

records.title: Self Portrait
records.lender: Lent by The Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, Philadelphia.
records.note: Inman was an excellent portrait painter with an amiable and good humored view of life. This interesting self-portrait gives an idea of the romantic artist at work but is unusually grave in tone for the cheerful Inman. Dated about 1831-34.

records.title: William Lloyd Garrison
records.lender: Lent by the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
records.note: Journalist, abolitionist. This mild-looking but implacable little New England reformer wrote in the first number of the Liberator "I shall strenuously contend for the immediate enfranchisement of our slave population . . . I will be as harsh as truth, and as uncompromising as justice. On this subject, I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation . . . I am in earnest—I will not equivocate—I will not excuse—I will not retreat a single inch—AND I WILL BE HEARD." Dated about 1845-47.
records.plate: Illustrated in the catalogue (in-text illustration, printed p. 10; PDF p. 13 of the HathiTrust scan)

records.title: Self Portrait
records.lender: The Detroit Institute of Arts, Detroit.
records.note: A talented, erratic, brooding, poetical artist who painted some of the best portraits of the period. He was a friend of Lowell and of the Brownings and spent eleven years in Florence and Rome, 1849-60, where some of his activities may be traced in the Browning letters. There he married a pupil, Sophie Candace Stevens, as his third wife and painted her portrait as well as his own at Rome in 1860.

records.title: Two Chiefs of the Kansas Indians
records.lender: Lent by The Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia.
records.note: Big Kansas, or Caussetonga (left) was described as inanimate and sleepy looking except on important occasions, but a dreadful opponent. He had a great friendship for Sharitarishe, chief of the Grand Pawnees, and would not consent to sit for his likeness without his friend. Sharitarishe was a distinguished orator, had great energy of character, and commanded great respect from his tribe. These Indians were painted at Philadelphia in 1821 while traveling as a deputation to Washington. Dated 1821.

records.title: Osceola
records.lender: Lent by The American Museum of Natural History, New York City.
records.note: Osceola was the leader of the Seminoles in their last war with the whites. He was a dangerous and implacable opponent of the United States in defense of the Seminole territory in Florida but a brave and generous foe. He was captured by treachery in 1838 and died a prisoner at Fort Moultrie. Dated painted in 1830's.

records.title: Mrs. Thomas Goulding
records.lender: Lent by the National Academy of Design, New York City.
records.note: The American romantic painters' interest in character is shown by their success with portraits of all kinds of people. They liked to paint mature old faces, thoughtful faces, interesting faces as well as handsome young people, and painted these mature characters with great understanding. Dated 1858.

records.title: Elizabeth at the Piano
records.lender: Lent by the Addison Gallery of American Art, Phillips Academy, Andover, Massachusetts.
records.note: Elizabeth was Elizabeth King Crowell. The Crowell family were close friends of the Eakins family and shared their musical tastes. Eakins painted a number of pictures of the two families which are masterpieces of the sympathetic portrayal of character and of the portrayal of the musician's absorption in his music. Dated 1875.
records.plate: Illustrated in the catalogue (in-text illustration, printed p. 12; PDF p. 15 of the HathiTrust scan)
records.plate_caption: 17. ELIZABETH AT THE PIANO by THOMAS EAKINS

records.title: The Chess Players
records.lender: Lent by The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York City.
records.note: The three old men in this dark nineteenth century drawing room in Philadelphia are the artist's father, standing, watching the game of two friends, M. Gardel (left) teacher of French, and George W. Holmes (right) printer and teacher. This might have been as appropriately catalogued under genre but the warmth and vitality of its characterization makes it also an interesting portrait group. Dated 1876.

records.title: The Conspiracy of Pontiac Revealed to Major Gladwin at Detroit by an Indian Girl
records.lender: Lent by The Burton Historical Collection of the Detroit Public Library.
records.note: In the spring of 1763 Detroit alone of all the English forts west of Fort Pitt withstood the onslaught of a great Indian uprising lead by Pontiac. All other fortified posts on the upper Ohio and the Great Lakes were taken by surprise and treachery. At Detroit Major Gladwin was warned by an unknown informant—no one knows exactly where the warning came from—and the fort withstood a long siege until relieved with great difficulty by a force led by Colonel John Montresor (whose portrait by Copley hangs in Gallery 28). Stanley, a Detroit painter, illustrates the popular legend that Gladwin was warned by a beautiful Indian girl who loved him, as it is told in Parkman's "Conspiracy of Pontiac." Dated 1863.

records.title: Naval Engagement Between the "United States" and the "Macedonian"
records.lender: Lent by The Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia.
records.note: The "United States" commanded by Decatur captured the "Macedonian," forty-nine guns, on October 25, 1812. The exploits of the tiny United States navy at sea and the battles of Plattsburg, Niagara and New Orleans (see Andrew Jackson) relieved the otherwise inglorious War of 1812 and made a great appeal to the popular imagination. Thomas Birch had been a portrait and landscape painter in Philadelphia until he was inspired by the naval battles of 1812 to paint a series of these gallant naval engagements. Dated painted in 1813.

records.title: Westward the Course of Empire Takes Its Way
records.lender: Lent by the National Collection of Fine Arts, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D. C.
records.note: This is a study for the large fresco painted in 1861 in a staircase of the Capitol, at Washington, in which Leutze attempted to create a monumental image of the great march to the Pacific. Dated 1861.

records.title: Scene in the First State Election in Michigan
records.lender: On loan, The Detroit Institute of Arts.

records.title: The Verdict of the People
records.lender: Lent by The Boatmen's National Bank of St. Louis, Missouri.
records.note: The rise of political party organization and party loyalties was not foreseen in our plan of government as it was originally conceived by its founders. The national political parties of today are a creation of the early nineteenth century. Bingham, a Missouri artist, was very actively interested in politics before painting this election scene. In 1848 he had been elected to the state legislature and in 1852 had been a delegate to the national Whig convention. He thus had first hand experience of the turbulent elections of those days when party loyalties were intense and the secret ballot unheard of. This picture was intended by the artist to be the climax of a series of paintings of election scenes and he wrote of it, "I intend it to be a representation of the scene that takes place at the close of an exciting political contest, just when the final result of the ballot is proclaimed from the stand of the judges. The subject will doubtless strike you as one well calculated to furnish that contrast and variety of expression which confers the chief value upon pictures of this class." Dated 1855.

records.plate_caption: 23. THE VERDICT OF THE PEOPLE by GEORGE CALEB BINGHAM

records.title: Prisoners from the Front
records.lender: Lent by The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York City.
records.note:
The national consciousness created by the first seventy years of the republic was put to its greatest test in the Civil War, 1861-65, when the interests of one region came into violent clash with the love of the Union. The instinct for unity won and decided that the vast new continent with all its diverse regions should be one country and one people. To foreigners the diversity of race and geography in the United States is so great that they wonder what holds it together—and, like Hitler, think it will easily fall apart under pressure. They do not remember that we fought and won a four year war as bitter, bloody and costly as any of modern times with the watchword, the Union must and shall be preserved.

Winslow Homer was attached for a time as war illustrator to the 61st New York volunteers, whose colonel Francis C. Barlow, is represented here interviewing prisoners. Homer represents the American soldier as we, too, know him—not a professional fighter but a civilian by instinct who does his dangerous and comfortless job well because it is his duty. Dated 1866.

records.title: Defiance — Inviting a Shot Before Petersburg, Virginia
records.lender: Lent by the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York City.
records.note: By the summer of 1864 the southern cause was lost but the magnificent Army of Northern Virginia fought on for a year longer in defense of the southern capitol. The nine months siege of Petersburg, which guarded the approach to Richmond from the south, lasted through the winter of 1864-65. Homer here depicts one of the incidents of the trench warfare with the keen observation, austere simplicity of form and sober force of feeling which characterize all of his work. Dated 1864.

records.title: The Veteran
records.lender: Lent by Miss Adelaide Milton de Groot, by courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York City.
records.note: This canvas painted in 1865 represents the emotions with which one great American artist saw the end of the Civil War. The sober power of his image of the returned veteran swinging his scythe in the harvest field, the originality of his approach and absence of sentimentality, give great dignity to his expression of an emotion which we all can understand today. Dated 1865.
records.plate: Illustrated in the catalogue (in-text illustration, printed p. 14; PDF p. 17 of the HathiTrust scan)
records.plate_caption: 26. THE VETERAN by WINSLOW HOMER

records.title: The Flight of Florimell
records.lender: The Detroit Institute of Arts.
records.note: Spenser's long, diffuse epic The Fairie Queene with its archaic beauty of imagery and moonlight quality was a favorite poem of two of the artists who best expressed this aspect of American romanticism, Allston the painter and Hawthorne the writer. Allston painted here an episode from Book III, Canto I, which happened as the Red Cross Knight and his companion were journeying through a dark forest. Dated 1819.
records.plate: Illustrated in the catalogue (in-text illustration, printed p. 15; PDF p. 18 of the HathiTrust scan)
records.plate_caption: 27. THE FLIGHT OF FLORIMELL by WASHINGTON ALLSTON

records.title: The Italian Shepherd Boy
records.lender: The Detroit Institute of Arts.
records.note: The impression Allston's reveries made upon the sensitive minds of his time may be realized from what Margaret Fuller later wrote about her first meeting with his pictures. "The calm and meditative cast of these pictures, the ideal beauty that shone through rather than in them, and the harmony of coloring were as unlike anything else I saw, as the Vicar of Wakefield to Cooper's novels. I seemed to recognize in painting that self-possessed elegance, that transparent depth, which I most admired in literature; I thought with delight that such a man as this had been able to grow up in our bustling, reasonable community, that he had kept his foot upon the ground, yet never lost sight of the rose-clouds of beauty floating above him. I saw too that he had not been troubled, but possessed his own soul with the blandest patience, and I hoped, I scarce know what, probably the mot d'enigme for which we are all looking. How the poetical mind can live and work in peace and good faith! how it may unfold to its due perfection in an unpoetical society!" Dated 1819.

records.title: The Court of Death
records.lender: The Detroit Institute of Arts.
records.note:
A hopeful movement toward mural painting of patriotic themes sprang up after the successful close of the War of 1812, but soon died out for lack of opportunity. Few public buildings offered wall space for murals and still fewer public bodies were ready to patronize the arts. The enthusiasm for large pictures then took a curious twist—artists painted huge pictures for the purpose of carrying them about the country, exhibiting them in hired halls and charging admission. The most famous and the most successful of these exhibition pictures was The Court of Death, painted by Rembrandt Peale in 1820. According to Peale's own statement, he took in $8886.00 in a little over a year from exhibiting this picture.

The idea was suggested by a passage in a poem on Death by Bishop Porteus. The elaborate allegory is as follows:

Death sits in the center, his foot on the corpse of a man in the prime of life, to illustrate his power over mankind. The head and feet of the corpse touch the waters of oblivion, to indicate the mystery surrounding the origin and end of life.

On either side of Death are his principal agents. On the right, War, Conflagration, Famine and Pestilence, rush over the fallen warrior and the widow and orphan.

On the left are Pleasure, who presents the cup to Intemperance, behind whom Remorse covers his face with his hands. Next are Delirium Tremens and Suicide. Beyond are a group of Consumption, Despair, Fever, Apoplexy, Hypochondria and Gout.

In front Old Age, supported by Faith, resigned but unterrified greets the figure of Death. Dated 1820.

records.title: The Voyage of Life — Youth
records.lender: Lent by St. Luke's Hospital, New York City.
records.note: The series of four paintings called the Voyage of Life were commissioned by the New York banker Samuel Ward, the father of "Uncle Sam" Ward and of Julia Ward Howe. It depicts first childhood, with the soul watched over by the good angel; youth (the present one) led astray by hope and pleasure; manhood, surrounded by storms and all the demons of destruction; and finally as old age enters the ocean of eternity in his shattered bark, his oars of self-reliance broken, helpless and repentant, the good angel returns once more to direct his gaze upward to heaven. The painting of pairs or series of compositions to tell a story of this kind, popularized by Cole, was very characteristic of romantic taste. The narrative element in painting, which produced the great fresco cycles of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, has never been fully acclimatized in American art. The first movement of romantic narrative painting (see Peale's Court of Death) was spent when Cole gave the impulse a different form and subject matter, which made it better suited to the taste and patronage of private individuals. In spite of its sentimentality The Voyage of Life reflects accurately the strongly ethical tone of American thought at that time. The exhibition of The Voyage of Life in Boston and New York with the artist's printed explanations caused a great sensation, comparable to the Armory Show of 1913 or the Rivera Frescoes in 1932. Dated 1840.

records.title: Wolfert's Will
records.lender: Lent by The Brooklyn Museum, Brooklyn.
records.note:
The illustration of subjects from romantic literature was less characteristic of American romantic painting than of European. But the genial humor and fantasy of Washington Irving's tales were the main inspiration of John Quidor. This is the last scene from "Wolfert Webber or Golden Dreams" in Tales of a Traveler. Wolfert was one of the placid Knickerbocker Dutch who were Irving's best comic characters. After terrifying and heartbreaking adventures while trying to find a pirate's buried treasure, Wolfert returned broken-hearted to die in poverty (as he supposed) on his ancestral cabbage farm in Manhattan:

He begged the lawyer to be brief, for he felt his end approaching and that he had no time to lose. The lawyer nibbed his pen, spread out his paper, and prepared to write. "I give and bequeath," said Wolfert faintly, "my small farm—"

"What—all" exclaimed the lawyer.

"Yes—all," said he.

"What! all that great patch of land with cabbages and sunflowers, which the corporation is just going to run a main street through?"

"The same," said Wolfert, with a heavy sigh, and sinking back upon his pillow.

"I wish him joy that inherits it!" said the little lawyer chuckling and rubbing his hands involuntarily.

"What do you mean?" said Wolfert, again opening his eyes.

"That he'll be one of the richest men in the place!" cried little Rollebuck.

The expiring Wolfert seemed to step back from the threshold of existence: his eyes again lighted up; he raised himself in his bed, shoved back his worsted red night cap, and stared broadly at the lawyer.

"You don't say so!" exclaimed he . . . "why, then I think I'll not make my will yet!" Dated 1856.

RICHARDSON (title page: THE WORLD OF THE ROMANTIC ARTIST — A SURVEY OF AMERICAN CULTURE FROM 1800 TO 1875 — THE DETROIT INSTITUTE OF ARTS — TWENTY-SIXTH LOAN EXHIBITION — December 28, 1944 — January 28, 1945). The pamphlet nowhere states Richardson's position at the Institute; no role beyond catalogue authorship is printed.

apparatus.index_note: The INDEX OF ARTISTS REPRESENTED (printed p. 35) as printed: 43 artists with the life dates the catalogue gives and their catalogue numbers. Reconciled against the catalogue body in both directions (audit, Nov 25, 2026): every number in the index resolves to an entry, and every entry is indexed under its artist — with one error, preserved as printed: the index also assigns no. 19 to William Page, whose line reads '3, 12, 13, 13a, 19, 78'; no. 19 in the body is John Mix Stanley's Conspiracy of Pontiac, and the index's own Stanley line correctly carries '19, 91'. Page's body entries are nos. 3, 12, 13, 13a and 78 only.

introduction.as_printed: An unsigned introductory essay (printed pp. 5–7) surveying the romantic period in American life: the growing national self-awareness of the first seventy years of the republic and its expression in three arts — architecture, literature and painting — the age of Emerson, Thoreau, Hawthorne, Irving, Poe, Melville and Whitman, and of the painters who made an imaginative record of the new nation, its people, its national life, its dreams and its experience of nature. It closes on printed p. 7 immediately before the first part heading, THE PEOPLE. Described, not transcribed.

apparatus.lenders_note: The LIST OF LENDERS page (printed p. 3; 39 lenders) as printed, transcribed in ordinary case from the page's small caps. Every lender in the list lends at least one work in the catalogue under its printed name except the New York State Historical Association, Cooperstown — see the notes: no. 81's entry names the Otsego County Historical Society, Cooperstown, which the list does not print. The Detroit Institute of Arts is not in the list: its own pictures carry its bare ownership line, and nos. 22 and 41, on loan to the Institute from owners the catalogue does not name, carry the line 'On loan, The Detroit Institute of Arts.' notes: The catalogue is written as a continuous illustrated essay, not a bare list: an unsigned introduction (printed pp. 5–7), then eight thematic parts, the entries embedded in the prose in numerical order. From no. 42 onward the prose commentary largely falls away and the entries stand as a compact list. The illustrations are printed in the text, each with a caption of catalogue number, title and artist; they are placed by subject, not by entry order, so a picture may be illustrated many pages from its entry (e.g. no. 95 is illustrated on printed p. 33, no. 92 on printed p. 31).

INDEX ERROR, as printed: the Index of Artists Represented assigns no. 19 to William Page as well as to John Mix Stanley. The body's no. 19 is Stanley's Conspiracy of Pontiac; Page's entries are nos. 3, 12, 13, 13a and 78. Both index lines stand as printed in the apparatus; the record stands under Stanley.
No. 58: the entry title prints 'Delaware Water Cap' (verified at 400 dpi) — a misprint for the Delaware Water Gap picture, preserved as printed.

Lender-name variants between the List of Lenders and the entry lines, all as printed: the entry lines habitually shorten the List forms, dropping state and city elements (the Fisher, Kesler, Lloyd and Ford lines end at 'Detroit' where the List prints 'Detroit, Michigan'; the Brooklyn Museum lines drop ', New York', the Museum of Fine Arts lines 'Massachusetts', the Walters lines 'Maryland', the Nelson Gallery line 'Missouri', the Cincinnati line 'Ohio', the Burton Historical Collection line ', Detroit, Michigan'). Substantive variants: the entry lines of nos. 14, 20, 50, 51 and 75 name 'The Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia' where the List names 'The Historical Society of Philadelphia, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania'; no. 1's line names 'The Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts' without the second 'the' that the List and the Academy's other entry lines (nos. 8, 11, 54, 78, 79) print; no. 21's entry line adds 'Smithsonian Institution' to the List's 'National Collection of Fine Arts, Washington, D. C.'; no. 60's entry line shortens the Addison Gallery's List form by dropping 'Phillips Academy'; no. 88's line adds a courtesy ('Lent by the Boston Athenaeum, courtesy of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston') and no. 26's adds one the other way ('Lent by Miss Adelaide Milton de Groot, by courtesy of The Metropolitan Museum of Art').

No. 81 is lent by 'the Otsego County Historical Society, Cooperstown, New York', a lender the List of Lenders does not print; the List's Cooperstown entry, the New York State Historical Association, lends no work under its printed name. The two stand as printed in both places.

The Detroit Institute of Arts is not among the List of Lenders. Its own pictures carry the bare line 'The Detroit Institute of Arts.' — no. 13a with ', Detroit' added, as are nos. 13 (by the shared line), 27, 28, 29, 39, 40, 42, 43, 62, 86, 91 and 96 — and nos. 22 and 41 carry 'On loan, The Detroit Institute of Arts.', the formula for pictures belonging to owners the catalogue does not name. Terminal full stops on these lines are inconsistently printed (wanting at nos. 57 and 74); lender lines generally want their full stop at nos. 45, 55 and 94 as well ('Lent anonymously' at no. 94 against 'Lent anonymously.' at no. 84). The prose that follows nos. 16 and 24 is general essay — on the romantic painters' portrayal of character, and on the Civil War as the test of national unity, closing with a paragraph on Homer as war illustrator — rather than a description of the single picture; it stands as those entries' notes, where the catalogue prints it.

Index forms, as printed: 'Inness. George' with a full stop for the comma after the surname; 'Matteson, T. H.' where the body entry prints 'TOMPKINS H. MATTESON'; Burnham's dates given as 'active 1836', Leutze's as 'died 1868', Salmon's as 'c.1785—after 1840'. The Still Life introduction prints 'Osias Beet' (for Osias Beert), 'Ambrosius Bosschaert', 'in Galley 7' (sic, for Gallery 7) and both 'Raphaelle' and 'Raphael' for the elder Peale within one paragraph.

The catalogue prints no dimensions and no media anywhere; medium and size are empty in every record. It prints no prices and no buyers; buyer, offer_price and sale_price are empty in every record.

The part heading prints 'POETIC REVERY, FANTASY, THE IDYLL' while the introduction under it twice spells the word 'reverie'; both stand as printed (heading in the parts list, 'reverie' in the transcribed introduction).

parts.heading: The People
parts.introduction_as_printed: The romantic artists were intensely interested in people. Human individuality was a subject of great imaginative and aesthetic importance to them and portrait painting flourished. To a superficial glance American portrait painting resembles the English school from which it sprang; but there is a great difference—the English romantic portrait painters (Lawrence and his school) were interested in decorative elegance and were at their best in portraits of pretty women; the Americans were interested in character and were at their best in portraits of mature men and women. Their works are simple, direct studies of a personality. Usually they were decorative, too, but the sense of life and character was primary. The record they have left us of an emerging national character is of great interest.
parts.subsections: I. National Leaders (nos. 1–4); II. Elegance and Romantic Beauty (nos. 5–8); III. Talent (nos. 9–13a); IV. Character (nos. 14–18)

parts.heading: Poetic Revery, Fantasy, The Idyll
parts.introduction_as_printed: The romantic period in America was one of immense activity and practical achievement: the continent was peopled, forests were felled, hostile Indians fought off, towns and cities built, our huge distances conquered by cutting roads through the forests, building steam boats on the rivers, driving railroads across the continent. The country was alive with incessant practical activity, with restless moving of great numbers of people ever westward, with hammering and sawing and digging and sweating to build a new country and with all the busy mechanical ingenuity and invention that transformed an agricultural civilization into the America of the machine age. Perhaps as a counter to all this, the imaginative life of our artists (as of our writers) seemed to dwell upon quiet. A spirit of reverie and contemplation, a kind of twilight mood of reflection tinged with poetic fantasy or sentiment was one of the artists' contributions to American life. It was needed to balance the incessant activity by a restless, practical people in the struggle to overcome hardship and difficulties. The mood of reverie (which was even more marked in our literature) took in American romantic culture the place of the Gothicism and orientalism of European romantic art.

parts.heading: Religion
parts.introduction_as_printed: There was an important religious revival in the early nineteenth century. Deism and rationalism had been dominant during the eighteenth century period of Enlightenment, but following the violent turn given to rationalism by the French Revolution, there arose a quickened interest in religious belief. The revival of Christian belief in the early nineteenth century had a powerful effect on society both through the traditional and the theologically liberal churches. Here again the romantic artists offer a fresh and interesting interpretation of their time, bringing to the ancient themes of Christian art their romantic appreciation of the mysterious, the tragic, the venerable and the poetic.

parts.heading: Animals and Birds
parts.introduction_as_printed:
From the time of the first explorers' visit to this continent men were interested to describe the strange animals and plants of the new world. In the eighteenth century the colonies had produced some important naturalists.

But the romantic period, with its sympathy for nature and interest in every phase of life characteristically produced a remarkable group of painters of birds and animals. There was Alexander Wilson, who illustrated his American Ornithology with his own colored etchings. Titian Peale, one of the many artist sons of Charles Willson Peale, illustrated Joseph Bonaparte's American Ornithology. Rubens Peale, another brother, spent most of his life as manager of the family museums but in his eighty-third year painted the picture of Ruffed Grouse in the exhibit. The most famous of all, however, was John James Audubon, who put a dramatic energy and fire into his paintings of birds and animals that made his work unique.

parts.heading: Still Life
parts.introduction_as_printed: The importation of works of art from abroad began to achieve notable proportions in the early nineteenth century and the first notable collections of art, both public and private, were formed. Dutch and Flemish pictures formed an important part of the first collections and among them were a number of still life paintings by artists of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth century. These pictures—of the type of our paintings by Osias Beet and Ambrosius Bosschaert in Galley 7—were the inspiration of the first American still life painters, Raphaelle and James Peale. James Peale (1749-1831), the younger brother of Charles Willson Peale, and Raphael (1774-1825), the eldest son, established a tradition of still life painting in Philadelphia which lasted through the nineteenth century. Its last and greatest painter was William Harnett.

parts.heading: Landscape
parts.introduction_as_printed:
Let one of their poets speak for the attitude of the romantic generation toward nature.

"To go into solitude, a man needs to retire as much from his chamber as from society. I am not solitary whilst I read and write, though nobody is with me. But if a man would be alone, let him look at the stars. The rays that come from those heavenly worlds will separate between him and what he touches. One might think the atmosphere was made transparent with this design, to give man, in the heavenly bodies, the perpetual presence of the sublime. Seen in the streets of cities, how great they are! If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and adore; and preserve for many generations the remembrance of the city of God which had been shown! But every night come out these envoys of beauty, and light the universe with their admonishing smile.

"The stars awaken a certain reverence, because though always present, they are inaccessible; but all natural objects make a kindred impression, when the mind is open to their influence . . . Nature never became a toy to a wise spirit. The flowers, the animals, the mountains, reflected the wisdom of his best hour, as much as they had delighted the simplicity of his childhood . . .

"To speak truly, few adult persons can see nature. Most persons do not see the sun. At least they have a very superficial seeing. The sun illuminates only the eye of the man, but shines into the eye and the heart of the child. The lover of nature is he whose inward and outward senses are still truly adjusted to each other; who has retained the spirit of infancy even into the era of manhood. His intercourse with heaven and earth becomes part of his daily food."—Ralph Waldo Emerson, Nature, 1836.

The love of that "intercourse with heaven and earth" produced in the romantic period our first school of landscape painters. Their delight in nature extended from the simplest to the most remarkable, awe-inspiring aspects of nature.
parts.subsections: I. The Wilderness Continent (nos. 42–47); II. The Seas and Ships (nos. 48–49); III. The Cities of America (nos. 50–53); IV. The Pastoral or Inhabited Landscape (nos. 54–60); V. The Exotic Landscape (nos. 61–74)

parts.heading: Life, Manners, The Variety of the Human Scene, The Humors and Flavors of Life
parts.introduction_as_printed:
American life was never more rich in materials for the genre painter, for the observer of human nature in its daily variety, than in the romantic period. The country was extraordinarily diverse. Costume ranged from the settled elegance of Philadelphia and Baltimore merchants to the coonskin cap and buckskin shirt of the frontier. Manners were equally picturesque and varied. Local differences had not been flattened out by ease of travel and communication—the New England Yankee, the Southern planter, the Western riverman ("half-horse, half-alligator, a little touched with the snapping turtle"), the farmer and the frontiersman and the untamed Indian, retained their pronounced local character. Powdered hair and knee breeches were still being worn when the period began; before it ended black-coated uniformity of business dress had settled upon mankind and artists had begun to go far afield in search of variety.

Humor was one of the first characteristic traits to make itself felt but a deep and quiet affection and a strange kind of grand and solemn poetry are also moods of our romantic genre.
